Trained in Paris, admired in São Paulo and ignored for decades by the museums of the north, Tarsila became a defining figure of modern art.
She painted not what Paris expected, not what São Paulo remembered, but what neither had imagined.
Neither a copy of Europe nor a rejection of it, her work was something new.
If the old map was wrong, if the center was never single, if the edges were never silent, then the story of modern art must be rewritten.
Several colleges ask about your background or community. Have you thought about writing about Brazil?
I have, but I worry it will sound like a travel brochure. Beaches, colors, samba.
That is a real risk. Admissions readers see a lot of essays that exoticize the writer's own country.
So what is the alternative? Pretend I am from nowhere?
No. Use it as a way of seeing, not as scenery. What do you notice in an American museum that your classmates here would not?
That the Latin American room is always small and always at the end, and that Tarsila is usually labeled as influenced by someone French.
Now that is an essay. It is not about where you are from. It is about what where you are from lets you see.
Neither a postcard nor an apology, but an argument.

Welcome to this room, which I have to admit is the one I argued hardest for. For a long time, when museums in this country showed Tarsila do Amaral at all, they presented her mainly as a student of French painters, as if her importance were something she had brought back from Paris in her luggage. I want you to look at these paintings differently. Notice how she takes the structure she learned in Europe, the clean geometry, the flattened space, and fills it with things no Parisian painter was looking at: the colors of houses in small Brazilian towns, cacti, palm trees, hills and figures from her own country. Now, you may have noticed that we did not put this room at the end of the exhibition, after the Europeans, as a kind of postscript. We put her here, in the middle. That choice is an argument. It suggests that modern art did not have one center that everyone else copied. It had several, and they were talking to each other.

Let's talk about a week that is famous in Brazil and almost unknown in American textbooks. In February 1922, at the Municipal Theater in São Paulo, a group of young writers, musicians and painters organized what they called a Modern Art Week. It was the year of the centennial of Brazilian independence, and the timing was not an accident. The events were chaotic. Some concerts were interrupted by booing, some lectures were mocked, and many people in the audience clearly thought the whole thing was a joke. Now, here is a detail that surprises many students, including Brazilian ones. Tarsila do Amaral, who is now the painter most associated with Brazilian modernism, was not there. She was in Paris, and she joined the group only after she returned later that year. So why did the week matter, if it was so disorganized? Because it announced, publicly and very noisily, that Brazilian artists intended to be modern on their own terms, and not only as followers of Europe.
